column29: 08/04/2022    'You will need to show evidence of a negative COVID-19 PCR test completed 72 hours before departure to enter or travel through Angola as a visitor.    In addition to the above requirement, all arriving passengers are required to undergo a rapid COVID-19 test immediately on disembarkation from the plane. The cost of the test is approximately USD $20 and is payable by Angolan bank card and visa card on arrival. The test is undertaken in a hangar at the airport. It usually takes approximately 20 to 40 minutes, depending on the number of passengers being processed, but it is advisable to carry water and refreshments in case there is a long wait.    All departing passengers are required to show evidence of a negative COVID-19 PCR test completed 72 hours before departure from Angola.    If you’re fully vaccinated  If you’re fully vaccinated, you can enter Angola without needing to quarantine regardless of your reason for travel.    Only vaccines authorised by the European Medicines Agency or by the World Health Organisation are accepted. All passengers who are fully vaccinated and test negative on disembarkation are exempt from any quarantine requirements.    Any passenger (vaccinated or not) receiving a positive COVID-19 result will go immediately into mandatory quarantine at a government facility for observation and further testing.    Proof of vaccination status  Angola will accept the UK’s proof of COVID-19 recovery and vaccination record and proof of COVID-19 vaccination issued in the Crown Dependencies. Your NHS appointment card from vaccination centres is not designed to be used as proof of vaccination and should not be used to demonstrate your vaccine status.    If you’re not fully vaccinated  If you’re not fully vaccinated, you will need to undertake compulsory self-quarantine for 7 days before undergoing a further COVID-19 test. A negative test is required to obtain a Titulo De Alta (ALTA) from the approved health centre and to be discharged from quarantine.'    Website Archive: https://web.archive.org/web/20220408190251/https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/angola/entry-requirements

column43: Are PCR and/or antigen tests available for U.S. citizens in Albania? Yes  If so, are test results reliably available within one calendar day? Yes  Airport Covid-19 PCR test:  Tirana International Airport offers a Covid-19 PCR test for travelers. For more information, visit their website.  Public Health Labs:  Currently, to be tested for COVID-19 by the Albanian public health authority one must have symptoms and a recommendation from the public health authority’s family doctor.  However, private testing labs will perform a test for a fee, and no symptoms or a doctor’s recommendation is required (see details below).  If you have an Albanian social security number, you also have an assigned public health family doctor.  To learn who your public health family doctor is, call the help line at 0-800-4040 to find out.  Tests are free of charge if done by the Albanian Institute of Public Health (IPH).  Private Labs:  Individuals can also arrange private testing by going to a private testing lab. No symptoms or doctor’s order is required to arrange a private test, and no advance appointment is necessary.  According to the Albanian Ministry of Health and Social Protection, there are several private labs authorized to perform SARS-CoV-2 testing for administrative issues. For a full list, please see the Ministry of Health list here.    https://web.archive.org/web/20220121115604/https://al.usembassy.gov/updates_covid19/

column32: The government adopted two support packages in 2020 for people and businesses affected by the COVID-19 pandemic of a combined size of Lek 45 billion (2.8 percent of GDP) consisting of budget spending, sovereign guarantees and tax deferrals. The first package adopted on March 19, 2020 through a normative act had support measures of Lek 23bn (1.4 percent of GDP) through a combination of spending reallocations, spending increases and sovereign guarantees to support affected businesses. The key measures are: (i) additional funding for health sector in the amount of Lek 2.5 billion (ii) Lek 6.5bn for the support of small businesses/self-employed that are forced to close activities due to the COVID-19 pandemic by paying them minimum salaries (up to two in the case of family businesses with unpaid family members), doubling of the unemployment benefits and social assistance layouts. (iii) Lek 2bn of defense spending reallocated toward humanitarian relief for the most vulnerable which were not used, (iv) Lek 11bn (0.6 percent of GDP) sovereign guarantee fund for companies to access overdrafts in the banking system to pay wages for their employees for up to 3 months with an interest rate capped at 2.85 percent for a maturity of up to 2 years. The government will bear the interest costs. The second package adopted on April 15 2020, includes (i) Lek 7bn (0.4 percent of GDP) fund to pay for a one-off transfer of Lk40,000 to employees of small businesses affected by the pandemic not covered in the first package, employees of large businesses laid off due to the pandemic, and employees in the tourism sector; (ii) a sovereign guarantee of Lek 15 billion (0.9 percent of GDP) to provide loans for working capital for all private companies that were tax-compliant and solvent before the pandemic. The government will guarantee 60 percent of the loans, and interest are capped at 5 percent. As of November 3, almost 98 percent of the overall budgeted direct support measures had been paid out while the take up for the first guarantee scheme was 59 percent and for the second scheme 42 percent. A third smaller support package was adopted on August 13, providing an additional minimum wage to public transport workers who resumed work one month later than the rest. The measure costing Lk135m is accommodated within the existing transport budget.    The government has also adopted tax deferral measures allowing all large companies (except banks, telecommunication, public enterprises and other essential businesses) to defer payment of profit tax for the second and third quarter of 2020 in 2021. Tourism, active processing and call centers can defer payments for the rest of 2020 to 2021. Small businesses with turnover below Lk14m will not pay profit tax for the remainder of 2021.    In September, the government launched an employment promotion program, that aims to cover part of reemployment costs of those who lost their jobs during the lockdown. For formal sector employees the government will cover half of the wages (at the legal minimum level) and the full employers’ share of social contributions for the duration of the program (4 or 8 months). Informal sector employees who lost their jobs during the lockdown, will have the full cost of social contributions (employees and employers share) covered for one year if they formalize.    /web/20220301071254/https://www.imf.org/en/Topics/imf-and-covid19/Policy-Responses-to-COVID-19

column43: COVID-19 Testing:    Are PCR and/or antigen tests available for U.S. citizens in Albania? Yes  If so, are test results reliably available within one calendar day? Yes  Airport Covid-19 PCR test:  Tirana International Airport offers a Covid-19 PCR test for travelers. For more information, visit their website.  Public Health Labs:  Currently, to be tested for COVID-19 by the Albanian public health authority one must have symptoms and a recommendation from the public health authority’s family doctor.  However, private testing labs will perform a test for a fee, and no symptoms or a doctor’s recommendation is required (see details below).  If you have an Albanian social security number, you also have an assigned public health family doctor.  To learn who your public health family doctor is, call the help line at 0-800-4040 to find out.  Tests are free of charge if done by the Albanian Institute of Public Health (IPH).  Private Labs:  Individuals can also arrange private testing by going to a private testing lab. No symptoms or doctor’s order is required to arrange a private test, and no advance appointment is necessary.  According to the Albanian Ministry of Health and Social Protection, there are several private labs authorized to perform SARS-CoV-2 testing for administrative issues. For a full list, please see the Ministry of Health list here.  Hard copy letters of test results are provided within 24 to 72 hrs. You can arrange another method of delivery (e.g.: email or text) with the individual labs.  Stay home and contact the Albanian National Medical Emergency line at 127 if you believe that you have contracted the COVID-19 virus.  Wait for guidance before going to a medical facility.  More information can be obtained by calling the national green line at 0-800-4040 to find out.  Visit the website of the Albanian Ministry of Health and Social Protection and the Institute of Public Health for additional information.  For information on limited humanitarian exemptions, please review the CDC’s website.    https://web.archive.org/web/20220301065252/https://al.usembassy.gov/updates_covid19/

column55: COVID-19 Vaccine Information:    Has the government of Albania approved a COVID-19 vaccine for use? Yes  Are vaccines available in Albania for U.S. citizens to receive? Yes  Which vaccines are available in Albania?  According to Albanian health authorities, the government is currently administering Pfizer-BioNTech, AstraZeneca-Oxford, Gamaleya and Sinovac vaccines.  So far Albania has administered more than 1,500,000 doses of vaccines.  At this time U.S. citizens and other foreign nationals are not eligible to receive a vaccine locally unless they have an Albanian residency permit, an Albanian social security number, and are registered with the national health system. If you have a residency permit and an Albanian social security number, you can register for details about the vaccination process at e-albania.al. Once you register you will be contacted with more information about receiving the vaccine.  Visit the FDA’s website to learn more about FDA-approved vaccines in the United States.    https://web.archive.org/web/20220305212231/https://al.usembassy.gov/updates_covid19/

column12: Between the 1st and the 13th of January, the ACT Government encouraged residents to work from home where it suits the employee and the employer to do so. column21: During this period, the ACT Government’s website indicated that buses were running on a summer holiday timetable, with all other services (including Light Rail, Taxis, Hire Car and Ride Share Services) were operating as normal.  However, the ACT Transport website did detail a number of Covid-19 related changes to services including the mandatory wearing of masks for everyone aged 12 years and older, required CBR app Check-In, practicing of good hygiene, no cash on buses, required use of rear doors to exit buses, closure of front seats on buses, and encouragement of physical distancing where possible. column9: There were no government implemented closures of schools during this period, with both early childhood education facilities and schools permitted for campus learning. Higher Education and Training Facilities were also permitted to provide campus learning, however density limits (1 person per 2 square metres) were required in indoor settings. Additional Covid-19 risk mitigation strategies including required check-ins and practice of good hygiene were implemented.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220214065134/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/current-restrictions  https://web.archive.org/web/20220225015838/https://www.education.act.gov.au/public-school-life/covid-school-arrangements
column15: Representing a continuation of the existing policy, the following restrictions were in place between the 13th and the 28th of February;  For indoor and outdoor organised events, organisers must develop a COVID Safety Plan. The following restrictions also apply to large events;  •	Density limits of one person per two square metres will apply for all indoor spaces (excluding staff).  •	Events over 1,000 people must be ticketed or pre-registered (smaller events must use the Check in CBR app).  •	Events of between 1,000 and 2,000 people must submit their COVID Safety Plan to ACT Health.  •	Events and gatherings greater than 2,000 people must seek an exemption, in accordance with the COVID Safe Event Guidance.  Density limits were in place across a number of sectors including retail and hospitality settings.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220214065134/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/current-restrictions
column18: This is a continuation of prior policy. No limit on visitors to home, or on the number of people allowed at informal outdoor gatherings. Gatherings with more than 1000 people must be ticketed or pre-registered, those with 1000-2000 people must have a COVID-safety plan, and those with over 2000 people need an exemption to go ahead. https://web.archive.org/web/20220214065134/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/current-restrictions
column24: There are no stay-at-home requiments in place. This is a continuation of prior policy. https://web.archive.org/web/20220214065134/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/current-restrictions
column27: In a continuation of the prior policy response to COVID-19, there are no restrictions on interstate travel to the ACT. https://web.archive.org/web/20220214065134/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/current-restrictions
column29: Fully vaccinated Australian citizens, permanent residents and eligible visa holders can travel to and from Australia without needing to apply for a travel exemption, but must produce a negative PCR test.    From 21 February 2022, all visa holders who are fully vaccinated for international travel purposes can travel to Australia without a travel exemption. Unvaccinated visa holders will still need to be in an exempt category or hold an individual travel exemption to enter Australia.    Unvaccinated visa holders will require a valid travel exemption.  https://archive.ph/whXWa
column34: The ACT Government's post-eviction moratorium transition period was announced by Attorney General Shane Rattenbury MLA on 12th Feb 2022 as continuing until 11 May 2022. This means that tenants who fell behind on rent during the moratorium will continue to be protected provided they pay rent as it falls due. Additionally, those required to quarantine or self-isolate are also protected from being required to leave their rental property during the period of quarantine or self isolation. https://web.archive.org/web/20220312034615/https://justice.act.gov.au/renting-and-occupancy-laws/information-tenants-and-occupants-impacted-covid-19 https://web.archive.org/web/20220312034612/https://www.cmtedd.act.gov.au/open_government/inform/act_government_media_releases/rattenbury/2022/continuing-support-for-tenants-during-covid

column12: During this period, the ACT Government encouraged residents to work from home where it suits the employee and the employer to do so. A number of mandatory vaccination requirements in the following sectors were also enforced during this time;   • Residential aged care facility workers   • ACT school, early childhood education and care facility workers   • Hospital, hospice, Canberra Health Services facility and patient transport workers   • Disability support workers or aged care workers that provide in-home and community supports   Additionally, mandatory CBR check-ins and COVID Safety Plans (detailing physical distancing, hygiene and sanitisation practices etc.) were required in a large number of settings within the territory, including hospitality, personal service and fitness settings. No entry restrictions were imposed on visitors or guests that weren't fully vaccinated to workplaces. In an easing of restrictions, density limits were removed from all previously restricted businesses and activities.  https://web.archive.org/web/20211221121302/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/stay-safe-and-healthy/vaccine/information-for-employees-that-require-vaccination#Which%20employment%20sectors%20require%20vaccination%20in%20the%20ACT?   https://web.archive.org/web/20220225015834/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/current-restrictions  https://web.archive.org/web/20220218003325/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/news-articles/public-health-measures-to-ease-across-the-act-from-tonight

column9: As reported by the ACT Government, no educational facilities within the ACT were mandatorily closed during this period. In schools, including early childhood facilities, a range of measures were introduced (throughout term 1)  to reduce risks of COVID, including requirements for staff and visitors to use check-ins, and for all staff, visitors, children, and young people to practice good hygiene. Higher education facilities are also open. Density limits at these facilities no longer apply at these facilities (since 18 Feb 2022), according to a media release from Andrew Barr MLA on 18 Feb.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220311043707/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/current-restrictions https://web.archive.org/web/20220311044359/https://www.cmtedd.act.gov.au/open_government/inform/act_government_media_releases/barr/2022/public-health-measures-to-ease-across-the-act-from-tonight
column12: As published by the ACT Government, return to work is allowed "where it suits employees and employers". Mandatory check-in is required at licensed bars and pubs, registered clubs, nightclubs, strip clubs, and brothels. Certain businesses, such as places of worship and businesses and venues that host funerals or weddings, must produce COVID-safety plans which include policies in relation to matters like physical distancing, hygiene, and managing staff or patrons presenting with illness. column15: A media release by Andrew Barr MLA shows that starting 25 Feb 2022, exemption requirements for all events were removed, meaning they are allowed to go ahead without restrictions on the number of people. However, events of over 5000 people still have to submit a COVID-Safety plan to ACT Health for review. Events that are not ticketed or pre-registered also have to use check-in processes. This is a relaxation of the prior policies, as exemptions are no longer required, density limits have been removed and fewer events have to submit COVID safety plans. https://web.archive.org/web/20220312013815/https://www.cmtedd.act.gov.au/open_government/inform/act_government_media_releases/barr/2022/public-health-measures-to-ease-across-the-act-from-tonight https://web.archive.org/web/20220312010628/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/current-restrictions

Exemptions are no longer required and the processes for holding gatherings have been relaxed.  https://web.archive.org/web/20220312010628/https://www.covid19.act.gov.au/restrictions/current-restrictions

column9: As published at 4 February 2022, there are measures for schools operations for Term 1 in 2022 from January 2022. The policy was implemented across ACT. The policy relates to arrangements for cohorting classes or year groups, improving ventilation measures, requirements for COVID-19 vaccinations for staff and other measures such as staggering the usage of resources and social spaces. column32: According to the Services Australia website (as last updated on 20 January 2022), eligible Australians who suffered financial hardship because they were required to quarantine or self-isolate as a result of having COVID-19, being a close contact of someone with COVID-19, or caring for someone who was required to quarantine or self-isolate were able to receive the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment or the Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19).     The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment could be received by individuals who were not receiving any income support payments, were not able to access paid leave entitlements, and had less than $10,000 (AUD) in liquid assets.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation after 18 January 2022 could receive $450 if they had lost between 8 hours (or a full day's work) and 20 hours of work, or $750 if they had lost more than 20 hours of work.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation between 9 December 2021 and 17 January 2022 could receive $750 for each 7-day period of quarantine or isolation.  Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation before 8 December 2021 could receive $1500 for each 14-day period of quarantine or isolation.     The Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19) could be granted to individuals who were receiving or eligible for an income support payment or the ABSTUDY Living Allowance, and were experiencing severe financial hardship. It was equal to a week's pay at the maximum basic rate of the recipient's income support payment or allowance. Individuals could claim a maximum of 2 payments during a 6-month period, or a maximum of one payment per isolation period.     A 50% reduction in the minimum superannuation drawdown rate which was implemented by the Federal Government in May 2021 continued to be in place.     The directions in place between on the 22 Janurary to 30 Janurary were a continuation of existing directions. Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation before 8 December 2021 could receive $1500 for each 14-day period of quarantine or isolation.    The Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19) could be granted to individuals who were receiving or eligible for an income support payment or the ABSTUDY Living Allowance, and were experiencing severe financial hardship. It was equal to a week's pay at the maximum basic rate of the recipient's income support payment or allowance. Individuals could claim a maximum of 2 payments during a 6-month period, or a maximum of one payment per isolation period.    A 50% reduction in the minimum superannuation drawdown rate which was implemented by the Federal Government in May 2021 continued to be in place.    The directions in place between 30 January and 5 February 2022 were a continuation of existing directions. column43: When should I get a COVID-19 test?  - You have COVID-19 symptoms. column58: As of the 25th of March 2022, extensive rules for visitors to aged care facilities have been put into place, these include;   1. An exemption to the Public Health (COVID-19 Care Services) Order 2022 has been signed to allow unvaccinated visitors to a resident who is at the end of life:  The exemption is subject to the condition that the operator of the facility takes reasonable steps to ensure:  no more than 4 people (including children) visit at any one time  all visitors wear a mask while in an indoor area, unless the visitor is interacting with the resident they are visiting  there is minimal interaction between the visitors and the staff and other residents  The visitors in this circumstance do not need to be vaccinated, however appropriate care must be taken if unvaccinated visitors are entering the facility. column32: According to the Services Australia website (as last updated on 20 January 2022), eligible Australians who suffered financial hardship because they were required to quarantine or self-isolate as a result of having COVID-19, being a close contact of someone with COVID-19, or caring for someone who was required to quarantine or self-isolate were able to receive the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment or the Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19).     The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment could be received by individuals who were not receiving any income support payments, were not able to access paid leave entitlements, and had less than $10,000 (AUD) in liquid assets.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation after 18 January 2022 could receive $450 if they had lost between 8 hours (or a full day's work) and 20 hours of work, or $750 if they had lost more than 20 hours of work.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation between 9 December 2021 and 17 January 2022 could receive $750 for each 7-day period of quarantine or isolation.  Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation before 8 December 2021 could receive $1500 for each 14-day period of quarantine or isolation.     The Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19) could be granted to individuals who were receiving or eligible for an income support payment or the ABSTUDY Living Allowance, and were experiencing severe financial hardship. It was equal to a week's pay at the maximum basic rate of the recipient's income support payment or allowance. Individuals could claim a maximum of 2 payments during a 6-month period, or a maximum of one payment per isolation period.     A 50% reduction in the minimum superannuation drawdown rate which was implemented by the Federal Government in May 2021 continued to be in place.     The directions in place between on the 22 Janurary to 30 Janurary were a continuation of existing directions. column32: Updated on 25 January, according to NT Government website:  The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is available for Territorians who can’t earn an income because they must self-isolate or quarantine for 14 days, or are caring for someone with COVID-19.    The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment is a lump sum payment of $1,500 to cover the 14-day isolation period.  A person can submit a claim for each 14-day period for which they have been told by a Territory health official to self-isolate and are unable to attend work and earn income.  Only one payment can be made in relation to each eligible 14-day period.  The payment is exempt from all Australian Government means testing and is taxable.  Services Australia is responsible for the service delivery of the Payment. The eligibility criteria is outlined on Services Australia’s website and guidelines are available on GrantConnect.  The cost of the Payment will be shared – the Australian Government is covering the administrative costs and costs for Australian residents and the Northern Territory is covering the cost for temporary visa holders.    Main resource: NT Government website    Archived:  http://web.archive.org/web/20220305161701/https://coronavirus.nt.gov.au/business-and-work/wellbeing-support
column34: On 24 April 2020, the Northern Territory Parliament passed the Tenancies Legislation Amendment Act 2020. This provides the framework for the Territory’s response to tenancy issues arising as a result of the COVID-19 emergency.    This fact sheet provides an overview of what you should do if you are struggling to pay rent.    -Get your documents in order  -Pay if you can  This period of time will not be a rent holiday. Rent unpaid will be money you owe your landlord. However, if you show your landlord you are in hardship, you will have additional time before the landlord can pursue termination.  -Raise your situation with your landlord  Many landlords are keen to help tenants get through this situation.  Talk to your landlord as soon as possible and make them aware of your situation. You could provide them with a copy of this document and the information sheet for landlords.    Main resource: NT Government website    Archived:  http://web.archive.org/web/20220305184148/https://consumeraffairs.nt.gov.au/rental-changes-due-to-covid-19/residential-tenants-affected-by-covid-19

column32: As of 29 March 2022, the Australian Government continued to offer Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment (PLDP) for eligible workers. People who are unable to work and lost at least 8 hours or a full day’s work in a 7 day period of self-isolation, quarantine, or caring are eligible for this PLDP.   For each 7 day period of self-isolation, quarantine, or caring, people would receive $450 if they've lost at least 8 hours or a full day’s work, and less than 20 hours of work; or $750 if they've lost 20 hours or more of work.  According to Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS; 2022), the median weekly earnings in Australia were $1,209.00 for all employees, and the median hourly earnings were at $36 per hour. Therefore, the amount of income support was greater than 50% median salary.      https://web.archive.org/web/20220411153734/https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/how-much-pandemic-leave-disaster-payment-you-can-get?context=53117  https://web.archive.org/web/20220411153807/https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/earnings-and-working-conditions/employee-earnings/aug-2021

column52: According to the Queensland Government, from Sunday 2 January 2022, you must wear a mask indoors everywhere in Queensland. This includes:  -	all indoor workplaces  -	public transport and rideshare  -	supermarkets and retail shops  -	hospitality venues including pubs, clubs and cafes  -	cinemas and theatres  -	indoor stadium, sports arena or sports centre  -	gyms and sport activities  -	vulnerable settings like hospitals and aged care  -	schools, childcare and other education facilities  -	airports and on planes    You do not need to wear a mask outdoors if you can remain 1.5 metres away from others that are not members of your household.    Children under 12 years and people affected by a medical condition or disability do not lawfully have to wear a face mask.    It requires people to wear masks outside the home in Queensland in some circumstances. For example, in some specified shared/public spaces outside the home with other people (who aren't members of their households) present, or some situations when social distancing is not possible.    Therefore, it should be reported as 2G. column32: According to the Services Australia website (as last updated on 20 January 2022), eligible Australians who suffered financial hardship because they were required to quarantine or self-isolate as a result of having COVID-19, being a close contact of someone with COVID-19, or caring for someone who was required to quarantine or self-isolate were able to receive the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment or the Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19).    The Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment could be received by individuals who were not receiving any income support payments, were not able to access paid leave entitlements, and had less than $10,000 (AUD) in liquid assets.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation after 18 January 2022 could receive $450 if they had lost between 8 hours (or a full day's work) and 20 hours of work, or $750 if they had lost more than 20 hours of work.   Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation between 9 December 2021 and 17 January 2022 could receive $750 for each 7-day period of quarantine or isolation.  Those claiming the payment for periods of mandatory isolation before 8 December 2021 could receive $1500 for each 14-day period of quarantine or isolation.    The Crisis Payment for National Health Emergency (COVID-19) could be granted to individuals who were receiving or eligible for an income support payment or the ABSTUDY Living Allowance, and were experiencing severe financial hardship. It was equal to a week's pay at the maximum basic rate of the recipient's income support payment or allowance. Individuals could claim a maximum of 2 payments during a 6-month period, or a maximum of one payment per isolation period.    A 50% reduction in the minimum superannuation drawdown rate which was implemented by the Federal Government in May 2021 continued to be in place.    The directions in place between 30 January and 5 February 2022 were a continuation of existing directions. column9: As of 7 February, QLD department of education has put in place the Back To School Plan 2022, for the period 7 February – 4 March 2022. Key features of the plan include:  •	Priority access to Rapid Antigen Tests (RATs) at Queensland Health testing clinics  for students and staff who have COVID-19 symptoms.  •	RATs available in schools for students and staff who develop symptoms while on site.  •	Mandatory mask wearing for staff in all schools, and all high school students.  •	Masks supplied and strongly encouraged for students in Years 3 to 6.  •	Suspension of school camps, excursions, assemblies, and large gatherings.  •	Limiting visitors on school sites, with exceptions for parents and carers of students experiencing vulnerability, and all students attending Early Childhood Development Programs, Kindergarten, Prep or Year 1 students.  •	Limiting face-to-face staff meetings, professional development, and face-to-face parent-teacher interviews.  These restrictions are in addition to existing measures including hygiene measures, cleaning, physical distancing and ventilation as described on the “Creating a COVID safe environment” department of education page.  Schools and other early childhood service providers are encouraged to stay open with restrictions in place. column9: Students are expected to be learning on school sites.    Same day student absence notification ( departmental employees only) requirements apply. Schools must notify parents or carers of an unexplained absence of their child as soon as practicable on the day of absence.    While students are learning onsite, schools are not required to provide home-based learning options unless there are specific circumstances justifying the student's absence.    Students unable to attend school because they are a close contact of a positive case of COVID-19 and following Queensland Health quarantine requirements  are not expected to do schoolwork while in quarantine. However, schools may choose to provide access to learning resources (such as learning@home ) to help students to continue their learning.    Students unable to attend school or participate in the learning program due to medical reasons should be supported by their school, just as they would be in the case of any extended medical absence. The school's approach to learning for the student should consider the expected duration of absence, the student's learning needs, available tools and resources, and the school's established approach to supporting continuity of learning.    At all times, including where a student is learning@home, any concerns of risk of harm to the student must be addressed in line with the department's student protection procedures. All student protection measures and training for staff and visitors must be maintained at all times.    Students of all ages are able to attend school regardless of their vaccination status. Any student over 16 years of age is not required to be vaccinated in order to attend school. Schools and students need to follow the heath directions for work placements and/or traineeships. column55: Who can get the COVID-19 vaccine?  - Children aged 5 to 11 can receive the Pfizer (Comirnaty) COVID-19 vaccine.  - All people aged 12 and over can receive the Pfizer (Comirnaty) or Moderna (Spikevax) COVID-19 vaccine.  - Adults aged 18 and over can receive the Pfizer (Comirnaty), Moderna (Spikevax) or Novavax (Nuvaxovid) COVID-19 vaccine.  - Adults aged 60 years and over can receive the AstraZeneca (Vaxzevria) COVID-19 vaccine. This is based both on the increased risk of complications from COVID-19 with increasing age (and thus increased benefit of vaccination) and the potentially lower risk of the rare side effect Thrombosis with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (TTS) with increasing age.    AstraZeneca (Vaxzevria) COVID-19 vaccine can still be used for people aged under 60 years if:  - you have already received your first dose without any serious side effects  - the benefits are likely to outweigh the risks for you  - you have made an informed decision based on an understanding of the risks and benefits.    How much does the vaccine cost?  The vaccine is free of charge to all Australians. Vaccination providers cannot charge you for the COVID-19 vaccine or for your appointments to receive the vaccine.    https://web.archive.org/web/20220324222109/https://www.qld.gov.au/health/conditions/health-alerts/coronavirus-covid-19/protect-yourself-others/covid-19-vaccine/about/about-the-covid-19-vaccine

column58: According to South Australia Health, a new direction came into effect on January 29th 2022, to limit entry into residential aged care facilities (RACF) in South Australia.    To enter a RACF:  - Visitors must have received at least dose of a TGA approved Covid-19 vaccination, and have evidence of a booking to receive a second dose.   - From January 29 2022, within four weeks of becoming eligible, you must receive a third dose (booster) of a TGA approved Covid-19 vaccine.  - Provide the operator of the RACF with proof of their vaccination status upon request.  - Exemptions: person have a medical certificate or a letter from a legally qualified medical practitioner certifying that the person had a medical exemption from receiving a Covid-19 vaccine, or they are child aged 12 years and 2 months or less.  - Upon entry, all visitors must wear a face mask over their mouth and nose (other than children 12 years or younger). Physical distancing of 1.5m should be adhered to wherever possible.    A person cannot enter an aged care facility if:  - You have had contact with a positive COVID-19 person within 14 days prior to entry  - You have a temperature higher than 38 degrees Celsius, history of fever or chills within the preceding 72hours, or have symptoms of acute respiratory infection or loss of taste or smell    Visitor limits:  - A resident of a RACF with more than 70% of its residents who have had at least one dose of a Covid-19 vaccine, there is no limit of care and support visits per day.  - A resident of a RACF with less than 70% of residents who have had at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine, may have one care and support visit of two persons or two separate visits from one person, per day. column58: According to South Australia Health, a new direction came into effect on January 29th 2022, to limit entry into residential aged care facilities (RACF) in South Australia. To enter a RACF:  - Visitors must have received at least dose of a TGA approved Covid-19 vaccination, and have evidence of a booking to receive a second dose.   - From January 29 2022, within four weeks of becoming eligible, you must receive a third dose (booster) of a TGA approved Covid-19 vaccine.  - Provide the operator of the RACF with proof of their vaccination status upon request.  - Exemptions: person have a medical certificate or a letter from a legally qualified medical practitioner certifying that the person had a medical exemption from receiving a Covid-19 vaccine, or they are child aged 12 years and 2 months or less.  - Upon entry, all visitors must wear a face mask over their mouth and nose (other than children 12 years or younger). column58: From the last update, March 3rd, 2022, South Australia Health has a number of covid safe measures requirement for entering Aged Care:    To enter a RACF:  - Visitors must have received at least dose of a TGA approved Covid-19 vaccination, and have evidence of a booking to receive a second dose.   - From January 29 2022, within four weeks of becoming eligible, you must receive a third dose (booster) of a TGA approved Covid-19 vaccine.  - Provide the operator of the RACF with proof of their vaccination status upon request.  - Exemptions: person have a medical certificate or a letter from a legally qualified medical practitioner certifying that the person had a medical exemption from receiving a Covid-19 vaccine, or they are child aged 12 years and 2 months or less.  - Upon entry, all visitors must wear a face mask over their mouth and nose (other than children 12 years or younger). Physical distancing of 1.5m should be adhered to wherever possible.    A person cannot enter an aged care facility if:  - You have had contact with a positive COVID-19 person within 14 days prior to entry  - You have a temperature higher than 38 degrees Celsius, history of fever or chills within the preceding 72hours, or have symptoms of acute respiratory infection or loss of taste or smell    Visitor limits:  - A resident of a RACF with more than 70% of its residents who have had at least one dose of a Covid-19 vaccine, there is no limit of care and support visits per day.  - A resident of a RACF with less than 70% of residents who have had at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine, may have one care and support visit of two persons or two separate visits from one person, per day.    Main source:  https://archive.ph/R33MP

column27: The Tasmanian Government updated its travel policy with new directions which came into effect at 12:01am on 1 January 2022:     	• All Australian states and territories (including LGAs which were previously considered 'low-risk') were considered 'high-risk'  	• All travellers who had been to 'high-risk' locations within 14 days prior to entering Tasmania, as well as unvaccinated travellers who had been approved to enter the state, were allowed to obtain a negative RAT result within the 24 hours before departure in order to enter Tasmania (instead of a negative PCR test in the 72 hours before departure). Individuals who had obtained a negative PCR test in the 72 hours before departure were still allowed to enter Tasmania provided that they had fulfilled all other entry requirements, but this was no longer essential. Travellers were generally required to quarantine until they could provide proof of a negative COVID-19 test.  	• However, there were no longer any testing requirements for individuals who had been outside Tasmania for 7 days or fewer - these travellers were required to take a RAT if they were symptomatic of a close contact of someone who had COVID-19.     With the exception of the classification of all Australian jurisdictions as 'high risk', these new rules were a relaxation of existing COVID-19 policy. Other interstate travel directions continued to apply:     According to the Tasmanian Government website (as of 23 December 2021), unvaccinated individuals (including Tasmanian residents, and excluding those with a medical exemption from taking a COVID-19 vaccine, as well as children under 12 years and two months) required approval in order to enter the state. They were only allowed to enter the state at approved ports, take COVID-19 tests on day 5 after arrival, and quarantine for either 5 or 14 days depending on the results of these tests.     All testing requirements for vaccinated and unvaccinated travellers applied to travellers 5 years old and over.     Fully vaccinated travellers who had not been to any high-risk locations in the past 14 days were exempt from all testing and quarantine requirements. Those from low-risk jurisdictions were able to transit at some approved locations in high-risk jurisdictions before entering Tasmania, without being subject to testing and quarantine requirements.     All travellers were required to register on the Tas-e-travel and scan QR codes on arrival. column45: According to a COVID-19 update published by the Tasmanian Government, Tasmania changed their definition of a close contact to match a nationally consistent definition of an individual who has "spent four hours or longer with a COVID-19 case in a household or household-like setting". This new definition came into effect on 1 January 2022, in light of a National Cabinet meeting which attempted to create a more unified set of guidelines for dealing with close contacts.    Individuals with COVID-19 were required to inform their close, social, and work/education contacts that they had been infected. Individuals with COVID-19 were to instruct their close contacts to self-isolate for 7 days, take a RAT on days 1 and 6 of isolation, and take a PCR test if symptomatic.    Those with COVID-19 were required to tell their social contacts to get a PCR test and self-isolate until receiving a negative result if symptomatic. A social contact was defined as an individual who the COVID-19 case had "15 minutes of face-to-face contact with, or spent 2 hours with, in the same indoor space".    Workplaces and educational institutions with COVID-19 cases were required to tell employees and students to get a PCR test and self-isolate until receiving a negative result if symptomatic.    These measures likely represented a relaxation of contact tracing efforts, as the narrower close contact definition, and the increased responsibility of COVID-19 cases to inform their contacts of the appropriate testing and isolation requirements, meant that public health officials spent less time communicating with COVID-19 cases and their contacts. column55: According to a COVID-19 update published by the Tasmanian Government, from 4 January 2022, individuals who were 18 years old and above were able to receive a COVID-19 booster vaccine at least four months after they had received a second dose of a COVID-19 vaccine. This represented a strengthening of previous directions regarding booster vaccines, which stated that individuals over 18 could receive a booster vaccine five or more months after receiving their second dose of a COVID-19 vaccine. The new directions came in response to advice from ATAGI to shorten the interval between the second dose and the booster dose in order to provide better protection against the Omicron variant of COVID-19.    All other directions regarding the Tasmanian vaccine rollout remained the same:    According to the Tasmanian Government website, COVID-19 vaccines were available, free of charge, for all Tasmanians who were 12 years old and above. The Pfizer (Comirnaty) and Moderna (Spikevax) vaccines were available to those 12 years and over, and the AstraZeneca (Vaxzevria) vaccine was available to those 60 years and over.  As 90.87% of all Tasmanians 12 years old and above had been fully vaccinated as of 23 December 2021, the Tasmanian Government had the capacity to fulfill its universal vaccine policy.    Some immunocompromised individuals could receive a third primary dose of a COVID-19 vaccine 2-6 months after their second dose. column15: There was no mention of a ban on public events on the Tasmanian Government website (as last updated on 4 January 2022, and current as of 20 January 2022). However, the Tasmanian Government developed a Framework for COVID Safe Events and Activities in Tasmania, which established regulations for different types of events depending on their level of risk, according to the Direction Under Section 16 - Mass Gatherings - No.6. In general, every individual at an event or gathering was required to maintain a physical distance of 1.5m from other patrons or staff where possible, and events were required to follow a density limit of 1 person per 2 square metres. Outdoor events with up to 500 people, as well as indoor events with up to 250 people, did not need to undergo further approval processes under the Events Framework, although they may have needed to create a COVID-19 workplace safety plan or conduct contact tracing as specified in existing directions for workplaces.     Tier 1 events, where the free movement of patrons was permitted, included indoor events with 251 - 2000 people, as well as outdoor events with 501-2000 people. These events were required to create an Event COVID-19 Safety Checklist and use the Check In Tas app for contact tracing. Masks were generally required at indoor venues and events with more than 1000 people attending.     Tier 2 events (all events with 2001 - 5000 people attending, where the free movement of patrons was permitted) and Tier 3 events (all seated events with 5001-10000 people attending, as well as higher-risk events) were required to create an Event COVID-19 Safety Plan, use the Check In Tas app, and apply for event registration. These events required approval before they could go ahead.     Unvaccinated patrons (i.e. those who had not received both doses of a COVID-19 vaccine at least 2 weeks ago) were prohibited from entering pubs, bars, nightclubs, outdoor events attended by over 500 people where visitors would be drinking while not seated, and indoor events attended by over 250 people where visitors would be drinking whilst not seated. Stadiums, arenas, theatres, cinemas, sporting clubs and community clubs were exempt from this requirement. Evidence of vaccination status could be provided through a COVID-19 digital certificate, Immunisation History Statement from the Australian Immunisation Register, or a similar document recognised by the Australian Government or Director of Public Health   The directions in place between 6 to 13 January 2022 were a continuation of existing COVID-19 policies. column18: According to the Tasmanian Government website (as of 4 January 2022 and current as of 20 January 2022), up to 100 individuals were permitted to attend gatherings at residential premises, including the usual residents of the premises.    The Tasmanian Government also developed a Framework for COVID Safe Events and Activities in Tasmania, which established regulations for different types of events depending on their level of risk, according to the Direction Under Section 16 - Mass Gatherings - No.6.    For gatherings outside of the home, organisers were to ensure that individuals were able to maintain a physical distance of 1.5m where possible, and a density limit of 1 person per 2 square metres. Masks were generally required at indoor venues and at outdoor events attended by over 1000 people.     Outdoor events with up to 500 people, as well as indoor events with up to 250 people, did not need to undergo further approval processes under the Events Framework, although they may have needed to create a COVID-19 workplace safety plan or conduct contact tracing as specified in existing directions for workplaces.    Tier 1 events, where the free movement of patrons was permitted,  included indoor events with 251 - 2000 people, as well as outdoor events with 501-2000 people. These events were required  to create an Event COVID-19 Safety Checklist and use the Check In Tas app for contact tracing.     Tier 2 events (all events with 2001 - 5000 people attending, where the free movement of patrons was permitted) and Tier 3 events (all seated events with 5001-10000 people attending, as well as higher-risk events) were required to create an Event COVID-19 Safety Plan, use the Check In Tas app, and apply for event registration. These events required approval before they could go ahead.    The directions in place between 6 to 13 January 2022 were a continuation of existing COVID-19 policies. column27: According to a media released published by the Tasmanian Director of Public Health on 6 January 2022, individuals were asked to reconsider their need to travel to King Island, and only travel to the island if absolutely necessary*. This announcement was delivered in response to a growing outbreak of COVID-19 on King Island, and represented a tightening of intrastate travel directions.    All other State Government internal movement directions remained the same (although travellers entering Tasmania were no longer provided with RATs from 7 January 2022 onwards):    According to the Tasmanian Government website (as last updated 6 January 2022 and 31 December 2021), all inbound travellers were required to register their trip via Tas-e-travel, and scan a QR code upon arrival.    Fully vaccinated travellers who had been to high-risk areas (all Australian states and territories outside of Tasmania) in the past 14 days were required to have a negative RAT taken within 24 hours before departure, or a negative PCR test taken within 72 hours before departure. Travellers who did not have evidence of a negative COVID-19 test taken within the required time periods were required to quarantine until receiving a negative test result. Vaccinated travellers who had not been outside Tasmania for more than 7 days were advised to take a RAT if symptomatic.    Vaccinated travellers could also transit directly through approved locations within high or extreme risk areas without needing to fulfill testing or quarantine requirements.    Unvaccinated travellers were prohibited from entering Tasmania unless they had received approval to enter for an essential reason. They were also required to have a negative RAT which was taken 24 hours before departure, or a negative PCR test which was taken within 72 hours before departure. Unvaccinated travellers were required to quarantine for up to 14 days after arrival, but could leave quarantine early if the mandatory COVID-19 test they took 5 days after arrival received a negative result.    *The C7 indicator was coded as 2G because the directions pertaining to interstate travel (2G) were stricter than those relating to intrastate travel (1T). column32: According to the Tasmanian Government website (as last updated 10 January 2022), eligible Tasmanians were able to access a range of income support payments offered by the Federal Government and the State Government.    The Federal Government was offering the Pandemic Leave Isolation Payment, a lump sum payment for eligible individuals who had lost income due to isolating or quarantining, or were caring for a dependent 16 years or younger who was required to isolate or quarantine.    The Tasmanian State Government offered a number of lump sum payments (Pandemic Isolation Assistance Grants) to eligible Tasmanians who lost income due to being affected by COVID-19:    Tasmanians who were unable to access the Pandemic Leave Isolation Payment could receive a Pandemic Isolation Assistance Grant if they were a close contact or a confirmed COVID-19 case who was required to quarantine and lost income as a result. These individuals could receive $750 dollars for each 7-day period for which they were required to quarantine, and an additional $750 (or a maximum total payment of $1500) if they needed to quarantine for an additional 7 days. The payment could also be claimed by individuals caring for a dependent who was a close contact or confirmed COVID-19 case.    Unvaccinated Tasmanians returning from interstate who lost income whilst undergoing mandatory quarantine were entitled to $750 for each 7-day period they were required to quarantine. This payment could not be claimed more than once within any 30-day period.    Individuals who missed work due to a public health direction to isolate whilst waiting for a COVID-19 test result could receive $250. This grant could not be claimed more than once within any 30-day period.    Tasmanians who lost income due to attending a COVID-19 vaccination appointment, due to experiencing side-effects of a COVID-19 vaccine, or due to caring for a dependent who was being vaccinated or experiencing COVID-19 vaccine side effects, could receive $250.     In order to claim any of the aforementioned payments, Tasmanians were required to demonstrate that they had lost income, had exhausted paid leave entitlements (or have no entitlement to such leave), and were not receiving any other forms of Australian Government income support.    The income support measures in place between 6 to 13 January 2022 were a continuation of existing COVID-19 policies. column43: According to media statements and press conferences conducted by the Tasmanian Premier between 6 and 7 January 2022, from 7pm on 6 January 2022 Tasmania moved towards using RATs as the primary diagnostic tool for COVID-19 . RATs would be free for individuals who were symptomatic or close contacts of a COVID-19 case (as well as those required to take a COVID-19 test under a public health direction), and positive RAT results could be registered online.     In a media release published by the Tasmanian Premier on 6 January 2022, the Premier mentioned that PCR testing would be available for those unable to use a RAT, those who had difficulty interpreting a RAT, and those who were clinically directed to take a PCR test. The Tasmanian Government website (as of 14 January 2022) also stated that PCR tests would be available to those who were unable to take a RAT, or were specifically instructed to take a PCR test. Individuals who obtained a positive RAT result and registered this result were considered to be confirmed COVID-19 cases, and symptomatic individuals who obtained a negative RAT result were advised to either take another RAT or a PCR test.    However, there were mixed messages pertaining to PCR testing eligibility. In a press conference on 7 January 2022, the Tasmanian Premier stated that individuals who were symptomatic or close contacts of a COVID-19 case could either take a RAT or PCR test. In this press conference, he mentioned that Tasmania's PCR testing facilities were all available, and that Tasmanians could arrange to book a test "if you want".     Therefore, although it is unclear whether Tasmanians who were symptomatic or close contacts could take a PCR test without fulfilling any other criteria in practice, the PCR testing directions in place between 6 to 13 January 2022 were a relaxation of existing policies. column45: According to the Tasmanian Government website (as last updated 5 January 2022) individuals with COVID-19 were required to inform their close, social, and work/education contacts that they had been infected.     Individuals with COVID-19 were to instruct their close contacts to self-isolate for 7 days, take a RAT on days 1 and 6 of isolation, and take a PCR test if symptomatic. A close contact was defined as an individual who has "spent four hours or longer with a COVID-19 case in a household or household-like setting".    Those with COVID-19 were required to tell their social contacts to get a PCR test and self-isolate until receiving a negative result if symptomatic. column12: According to a media update published by the Tasmanian Government on 13 January 2022, the Tasmania was creating a temporary exemption framework for close contacts working in critical industries. This framework enabled critical employees in essential business undergoing critical workforce shortages to apply for an exemption from isolation or quarantine requirements if they became close contacts of a COVID-19 case. The framework was available for businesses in the following sectors:   - Day procedures centres included in the Health Services Establishments Act   - Emergency services   - Power, utilities, and essential infrastructure services   - Agriculture and fisheries   - Freight and logistics involved in delivering essential goods   - Major manufacturing, distribution, and critical supply chains related to essential goods   - Correctional and detention facilities   - Essential commercial cleaning services   - Public transport services.     Before registering for the framework, businesses were required to assess the risks of a critical workforce shortage, seek possible alternatives to requesting close contacts to fill the shortage, and implement extra COVID-Safe measures such as increased testing of workers.     This update was a relaxation of existing COVID-19 policy directions. All other workplace restrictions pertaining to COVID-19 remained the same:     According to the Tasmanian Government website (as last updated on 4 January 2022) all businesses were permitted to operate, but were required to adopt measures to meet minimum COVID-19 safety standards as stated in the Direction under Section 16 - COVID-19 Workplace Plans - No.2, and record these in a safety plan. As part of these minimum safety standards, businesses were required to practice 1.5m social distancing or impose a density limit of 1 person per 2 square metres (although exempted workplaces were only required to ensure that the number of individuals in the workplace did not exceed the number specified on their occupancy permits), maintain cleaning and hygiene practices workplace to minimise the spread of COVID-19, train and inform staff and patrons of COVID-safe requirements they must follow in order to minimise transmission, prevent individuals who had COVID-19 symptoms or were known to be under isolation requirements from entering the premises, and collect contact information from individuals entering or leaving the workplace in order to assist with contact tracing efforts.     Masks were also required in indoor spaces. Individuals entering pubs, nightclubs, bars, and some licensed events were required to be fully vaccinated. Other industry-specific COVID-safe guidelines, such as regular COVID-19 testing for those working in quarantine facilities, and the adoption of transmission-based precautions  in healthcare settings were also in place. column15: There was no mention of a ban on public events on the Tasmanian Government website (as last updated on 4 January 2022, and current as of 20 January 2022). However, the Tasmanian Government developed a Framework for COVID Safe Events and Activities in Tasmania, which established regulations for different types of events depending on their level of risk, according to the Direction Under Section 16 - Mass Gatherings - No.6. In general, every individual at an event or gathering was required to maintain a physical distance of 1.5m from other patrons or staff where possible, and events were required to follow a density limit of 1 person per 2 square metres. Outdoor events with up to 500 people, as well as indoor events with up to 250 people, did not need to undergo further approval processes under the Events Framework, although they may have needed to create a COVID-19 workplace safety plan or conduct contact tracing as specified in existing directions for workplaces.     Tier 1 events, where the free movement of patrons was permitted, included indoor events with 251 - 2000 people, as well as outdoor events with 501-2000 people. These events were required to create an Event COVID-19 Safety Checklist and use the Check In Tas app for contact tracing. Masks were generally required at indoor venues and events with more than 1000 people attending.     Tier 2 events (all events with 2001 - 5000 people attending, where the free movement of patrons was permitted) and Tier 3 events (all seated events with 5001-10000 people attending, as well as higher-risk events) were required to create an Event COVID-19 Safety Plan, use the Check In Tas app, and apply for event registration. These events required approval before they could go ahead.     Unvaccinated patrons (i.e. those who had not received both doses of a COVID-19 vaccine at least 2 weeks ago) were prohibited from entering pubs, bars, nightclubs, outdoor events attended by over 500 people where visitors would be drinking while not seated, and indoor events attended by over 250 people where visitors would be drinking whilst not seated. Stadiums, arenas, theatres, cinemas, sporting clubs and community clubs were exempt from this requirement. Evidence of vaccination status could be provided through a COVID-19 digital certificate, Immunisation History Statement from the Australian Immunisation Register, or a similar document recognised by the Australian Government or Director of Public Health.   The directions in place between 14 and 21 January were a continuation of existing restrictions. column27: According to the Tasmanian Government website as of 13 and 14 January 2022, all arrivals were required to register their trip on Tas-e-travel, scan a QR code upon arrival, and have evidence of a vaccination certificate.    Vaccinated travellers (those who had received a full course of a COVID-19 vaccine at least 14 days ago, had a medical exemption from receiving a vaccine, or were under the age of 12 years and two months) were not required to get tested for COVID-19 if they had not visited a high or extreme risk location in the past 14 days. Those from low-risk areas who could undertake direct transit in an approved location at a high-risk jurisdiction were also able to enter Tasmania without needing to get a COVID-19 test or quarantine. Vaccinated travellers who had been out of Tasmania for 7 days or fewer were not required to quarantine or get tested for COVID-19, but were asked to get a RAT if they became symptomatic or were a close contact of someone with COVID-19.   Vaccinated travellers who had visited high-risk areas (all Australian jurisdictions) within the past 14 days could only enter Tasmania if they had a negative result from a PCR test taken within 72 hours before departure or a RAT taken within 24 hours before departure. Those who did not have a negative COVID-19 test result were required to quarantine until they were able to return a negative test.    Unvaccinated travellers could only enter Tasmania if they had received approval to do so for essential reasons, and  if they had a negative result from a PCR test taken within 72 hours before departure or a RAT taken within 24 hours before departure.   Approved unvaccinated travellers could only arrive via approved entry points. They were required to quarantine for a minimum of 5 days, and take a COVID-19 test on their fifth day in Tasmania. Travellers could leave quarantine if this test returned a negative result, but were required to quarantine for a total of 14 days if they received a positive result.    The directions in place between 14 and 18 January were a continuation of existing restrictions. column32: According to the Tasmanian Government website (as last updated on 10 January 2022), eligible Tasmanians who lost income for reasons related to COVID-19 were able to access a range of income support measures provided by the Federal Government and the Tasmanian Government.    The Federal Government offered the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment, a lump sum payment for some eligible individuals who lost income whilst isolating due to contracting COVID-19 or being a close contact of a COVID-19 case.    The Tasmanian Government offered several different assistance grants:    A $250 lump sum payment was offered to Tasmanians who lost income whilst isolating to wait for a PCR test result. This could only be claimed a maximum of once within a 30-day period.   Similarly, those who lost income as a result of receiving a COVID-19 vaccine, experiencing COVID-19 vaccine side effects within 3 days after being vaccinated, or caring for a dependant who had received the COVID-19 vaccine, could also receive a $250 payment.    Tasmanians who were unable to access the Pandemic Leave Disaster Payment, and lost income whilst  isolating due to contracting COVID-19, being a close contact of a COVID-19 case, or caring for a dependent who was a COVID-19 case or close contact, could receive the Pandemic Isolation Assistance Grant. This was a payment of $750 for every 7-day period of isolation, and Tasmanians could receive a total of $1500 if they were required to isolate for 14 days.    Those who lost income as a result of being required to quarantine after entering Tasmania could receive a $750 lump sum payment for each period of up to 7 days that they were in quarantine. This payment could only be claimed a maximum of once within a 30 day period.    Typically, Tasmanians could only be eligible for the aforementioned income support payments if they were unable to access paid sick leave or carers leave entitlements, and were not receiving any other form of Australian Government income support.    The income support measures available between 14 and 21 January 2022 were a continuation of existing relief measures. column55: According to the Tasmanian Government website as of 14 January 2022, the Pfizer (Comirnaty) and Moderna (Spikevax) COVID-19 vaccines would be available to all Tasmanians 12 years old and above, whilst the AstraZeneca (Vaxzevria) COVID-19 was available to those 60 years and above. column58: According to the Tasmanian Government website as of 21 January 2022, visitors were prohibited from entering residential aged care facilities if they had contact with a confirmed or suspected COVID-19 case within 7 days before entry. This was a relaxation of existing policies, which stated that visitors who had contact with a confirmed or suspected COVID-19 case within 14 days before entry were prohibited from entering.     All other directions pertaining to entry to residential aged care facilities remained the same:    According to the Tasmanian Government website as of 14 January 2022, visitors could only enter residential aged care facilities if they wore a mask, had no COVID-19 symptoms, were not required to quarantine or isolate, had not visited an exposure site in the past 14 days and were not required to avoid high-risk settings, and had checked into the facility. Visitors entering communal areas were also asked to maintain a physical distance of 1.5m from others where possible.    Individuals who were unable to provide proof that they had received both doses of a COVID-19 vaccination at least two weeks before entering a residential aged care facility (including those with a medical exemption, as well as those over 28 days old) were required to either have evidence of a negative PCR test taken within 72 hours before entry, or have evidence of a negative RAT taken within 24 hours before entry.    Staff and visitors were screened before entry to ensure that they had met all the aforementioned criteria. column9: According to the Tasmanian Department of Education website as of 28 January 2022, schools were operating as normal, in line with public health advice.     The website stated that schools would be operating under increased hygiene practices, with social distancing among adults (but not children), increased ventilation and outdoor learning spaces, the use of the Check in Tas app, and the wearing of masks (except by primary school students).     Students were also advised to stay at home if they were unwell, or were directed to do so due to a public health direction or a medical condition. The directions in place between 22 and 29 January were a continuation of existing restrictions. column12: The Tasmanian Government website (as last updated on 4 January 2022, and current as of 28 January 2022) stated that business were allowed to operate, but were required to implement measures to meet minimum COVID-19 safety standards and record them in a safety plan. According to the Direction Under Section 16 - Workplace COVID Plan - No.2, these minimum standards included the following:    	- Maintaining a physical distance of 1.5m where possible, or a density limit of 1 person per 2 square limits (unless the workplace was exempt from doing so)  	- Reviewing public health advice regularly in order to find ways to keep the business COVID-safe, as well as training workers to minimise the risk of COVID-19 transmission in the workplace, and informing patrons of COVID-related safety measures and restrictions  	- Cleaning and disinfecting the workplace as necessary to reduce the risk of COVID-19 transmission  	- Preventing individuals with COVID-19 symptoms, or those who are required to quarantine or self-isolate, from entering the business  	- Collecting contact information from individuals entering the workplace for contact tracing purposes (unless exempt from doing so)    Businesses were encouraged to review and update their Workplace COVID Plans as of 20 January 2022.    Masks were required in all indoor spaces and outdoor events attended by more than 1000 patrons, except where an individual had to perform a job that required clear enunciation or mouth visibility.    Unvaccinated patrons (i.e. those who had not received both doses of a COVID-19 vaccine at least 2 weeks ago) were prohibited from entering pubs, bars, nightclubs, outdoor events attended by over 500 people where visitors would be drinking while not seated, and indoor events attended by over 250 people where visitors would be drinking whilst not seated. Stadiums, arenas, theatres, cinemas, sporting clubs and community clubs were exempt from this requirement. Unvaccinated individuals were also prohibited from entering residential aged care facilities unless they had tested negative for COVID-19 (see H8 for more details). Evidence of vaccination status could be provided through a COVID-19 digital certificate,   Immunisation History Statement from the Australian Immunisation Register, or a similar document recognised by the Australian Government or Director of Public Health.    The directions in place between 22 and 27 January were a continuation of existing restrictions.    Note: Workers were required to be vaccinated at some businesses including quarantine facilities, health care settings, aged care and disability settings, and at licensed settings (such as pubs, clubs, bars, and nightclubs). Individuals working in early childhood education setting were required to have received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine from 8 January 2022. This information was not recorded in C2 or V4 as of 5 February 2022. column15: There was no mention of a ban on public events on the Tasmanian Government website (as last updated on 4 January 2022, and current as of 28 January 2022).    However, the Tasmanian Government developed a Framework for COVID Safe Events and Activities in Tasmania, which established regulations for different types of events depending on their level of risk, according to the Direction Under Section 16 - Mass Gatherings - No.6.    In general, every individual at an event or gathering was required to maintain a physical distance of 1.5m from other patrons or staff where possible, and events were required to follow a density limit of 1 person per 2 square metres. Outdoor events with up to 500 people, as well as indoor events with up to 250 people, did not need to undergo further approval processes under the Events Framework, although they may have needed to create a COVID-19 workplace safety plan or conduct contact tracing as specified in existing directions for workplaces.    Tier 1 events, where the free movement of patrons was permitted,  included indoor events with 251 - 2000 people, as well as outdoor events with 501-2000 people. These events were required  to create an Event COVID-19 Safety Checklist and use the Check In Tas app for contact tracing. Masks were generally required at indoor venues and events with more than 1000 people attending.    Tier 2 events (all events with 2001 - 5000 people attending, where the free movement of patrons was permitted) and Tier 3 events (all seated events with 5001-10000 people attending, as well as higher-risk events) were required to create an Event COVID-19 Safety Plan, use the Check In Tas app, and apply for event registration. These events required approval before they could go ahead.    Unvaccinated patrons (i.e. those who had not received both doses of a COVID-19 vaccine at least 2 weeks ago) were prohibited from entering pubs, bars, nightclubs, outdoor events attended by over 500 people where visitors would be drinking while not seated, and indoor events attended by over 250 people where visitors would be drinking whilst not seated. Stadiums, arenas, theatres, cinemas, sporting clubs and community clubs were exempt from this requirement. Evidence of vaccination status could be provided through a COVID-19 digital certificate, Immunisation History Statement from the Australian Immunisation Register, or a similar document recognised by the Australian Government or Director of Public Health.    The directions in place between 22 and 28 January were a continuation of existing restrictions. Tier 2 events (all events with 2001 - 5000 people attending, where the free movement of patrons was permitted) and Tier 3 events (all seated events with 5001-10000 people attending, as well as higher-risk events) were required to create an Event COVID-19 Safety Plan, use the Check In Tas app, and apply for event registration. These events required approval before they could go ahead.    Unvaccinated patrons (i.e. those who had not received both doses of a COVID-19 vaccine at least 2 weeks ago) were prohibited from entering pubs, bars, nightclubs, outdoor events attended by over 500 people where visitors would be drinking while not seated, and indoor events attended by over 250 people where visitors would be drinking whilst not seated. column27: According to the Tasmanian Government website as of 28 January 2022, fully vaccinated travellers (those who had received a full course of a COVID-19 vaccine at least 14 days ago, had a medical exemption from receiving a vaccine, or were under the age of 12 years and two months) would no longer be required to register their details or undergo COVID-19 testing in order to enter Tasmania. Although individuals who had been to extreme-risk areas in the past 14 days were required to obtain approval in order to enter Tasmania, as well as fulfill testing and quarantine requirements regardless of their vaccination status, there were no areas declared extreme-risk between 22-29 January 2022.    Unvaccinated travellers could only enter Tasmania if they had received approval to do so for essential reasons, and  if they had a negative result from a PCR test taken within 72 hours before departure or a RAT taken within 24 hours before departure.   Approved unvaccinated travellers were required to register their trip on Tas-e-travel, scan a QR code upon arrival, and arrive via approved entry points . They were required to quarantine for a minimum of 5 days, and take a COVID-19 test on their fifth day in Tasmania. Unvaccinated travellers could leave quarantine if this test returned a negative result, but were required to quarantine for a total of 14 days if they received a positive result.    The directions in place between 22 and 29 January were a continuation of existing COVID-19 policies.
